subtopics.name: Implementation fundamentals
subtopics.summary: Turning a statement directly into correct code: reading input fast, choosing the right integer type and handling every edge case. Almost every Div 2/3/4 A problem is pure implementation; the difficulty is precision, not ideas.
learn: Fast I/O: ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); never mix with printf/scanf after that
Know the limits: int ~2.1e9, long long ~9.2e18; use long long whenever a product or sum can exceed 2e9
Multi-test input (t test cases): reset all global arrays/counters per test, and respect 'sum of n over all tests' bounds
Read the statement twice; write down the exact output format (YES/NO case, spaces, -1 cases) before coding
Test on the samples plus hand-made edge cases: n=1, all equal elements, maximum values
Prefer simple, direct code over clever code; off-by-one errors are the main source of WA

resources.title: USACO Guide: Fast Input and Output

subtopics.name: Time complexity & constraint estimation
subtopics.summary: Estimating the running time of an idea from the constraints before coding it: roughly 1e8 simple operations per second. Reading n <= 2e5 should immediately suggest O(n log n), n <= 20 suggests 2^n, and so on.
learn: Big-O rules: loops multiply, sequential parts add, keep the dominant term
Constraint table: n<=10 -> O(n!), n<=20 -> O(2^n), n<=500 -> O(n^3), n<=5000 -> O(n^2), n<=2e5 -> O(n log n), n<=1e18 -> O(log n) or O(sqrt) on a smaller quantity
Iterate divisors up to sqrt(n): O(sqrt n) instead of O(n)
Bounded search: if the answer or a variable is at most cube-root/sqrt of the limit, brute-force over it
Watch hidden costs: string concatenation, erasing from vector front, endl flushing, copying containers into functions
Amortized analysis: a pointer that only moves forward costs O(n) total

subtopics.name: Simulation
subtopics.summary: Doing exactly what the statement describes, step by step, with the right data structures. Harder versions require noticing that the process repeats (cycle/period) or that only a bounded number of steps matter, so it can be fast-forwarded.
learn: Model the state explicitly (positions, grid, queue) and update it one step at a time
Use deque/stack/set when the simulation adds/removes from ends or needs ordered access
Grids: direction arrays dx/dy, boundary checks, and simulating gravity/rotations carefully
If the number of steps is huge, find a period (state repeats) or a point after which nothing changes, then jump ahead with arithmetic
Bound the number of 'interesting' steps (e.g. values shrink quickly, last digit cycles) and simulate only those
Write the simulation as a function and test it on the sample before optimising

subtopics.name: Casework
subtopics.summary: Splitting the input space into a few cases that are each easy to solve. Typical when the answer is a small number (0/1/2/-1) or depends on parity, signs or which of a few configurations occurs.
learn: Enumerate cases systematically (e.g. by sign, parity, which element is the maximum) so none are missed
Prove the answer is always small (e.g. at most 2 operations) and then check 0, 1, 2 separately
Brute-force small inputs to validate your case analysis
Handle degenerate cases first: n=1, all equal, already sorted, zero
When cases multiply, try to reduce them by symmetry (swap a,b; reverse the array)

subtopics.name: Brute force by iterating
subtopics.summary: Trying every candidate answer or every combination of a few variables with nested loops. Works whenever the search space, after bounding it smartly, fits in about 1e8 operations.
learn: Identify what to enumerate: the answer itself, a pair (i, j), a small parameter (k, a digit, a divisor)
Bound the search space with an observation (answer <= 60, only sqrt(n) divisors, only 2 distinct values matter)
Fix one variable and compute the rest greedily or with a formula
Check the total complexity across all test cases before coding
Brute force is also your testing tool: write it to validate a faster solution on random small inputs

subtopics.name: Recursion & generating candidates
subtopics.summary: Writing a recursive function that explores choices or divides a problem into self-similar halves. Used to generate all numbers of a special form, to check divide-and-conquer structures, or to try both options at each step.
learn: Define the state passed to the recursion and the base case first
Generate special numbers (e.g. made only of digits 4/7) recursively instead of looping over all integers
Divide and conquer on halves: solve(l, r) splits into solve(l, mid) and solve(mid+1, r)
Count the recursion tree size to estimate complexity (branching^depth)
Watch the recursion depth (default stack ~ 1e5-1e6 frames); convert to iteration if needed

resources.title: USACO Guide: Complete Search with Recursion

subtopics.name: Generating subsets (bitmask enumeration)
subtopics.summary: Enumerating all 2^n subsets of a small set, usually with an integer mask from 0 to 2^n - 1. Appears when n <= 20 or when the choice per element is binary and few elements matter.
learn: Loop mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1; element i is chosen iff (mask>>i)&1
Recursive alternative: at each index either take or skip the element
Iterate all submasks of a mask: for (s = m; s; s = (s-1) & m) — total 3^n over all masks
Enumerate over a small 'type' set (e.g. which of 26 letters are allowed, which corners are filled) even when n itself is large
Complexity O(2^n * n); for n around 40 switch to meet-in-the-middle

resources.title: USACO Guide: Complete Search with Recursion (Subsets)
cp-algorithms: Enumerating submasks of a bitmask

subtopics.name: Generating permutations
subtopics.summary: Trying all n! orderings with next_permutation or recursion when n <= 8-10. Also used to enumerate all digit orders or all assignments of distinct roles.
learn: Sort first, then do { ... } while (next_permutation(a.begin(), a.end())) to visit each permutation once (handles duplicates)
Recursive generation with a used[] array when you need pruning
n! grows fast: 8! = 40320, 10! ~ 3.6e6, 11! ~ 4e7 — check limits
Often you permute a small 'pattern' (digit positions, 5 people, 3 rectangles) rather than the whole input
Combine with a cheap evaluation per permutation; total cost is n! times evaluation

resources.title: USACO Guide: Complete Search with Recursion (Permutations)

subtopics.name: Backtracking & pruning
subtopics.summary: Building a solution incrementally and abandoning a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer. Pruning (and memoization) turns an exponential search into something fast enough in practice.
learn: Template: place(i): if i==n record answer; for each choice c valid at i: apply c, place(i+1), undo c
Prune early: check constraints as soon as a choice is made, not only at the end
Prune by bounds: stop if the current partial cost already exceeds the best answer
Symmetry breaking: fix the first choice to cut identical branches
When the same state repeats, memoize it — this is the bridge to dynamic programming
Classic examples: n-queens, grid path counting with dead-end detection, generating numbers with digit constraints

resources.title: USACO Guide: Complete Search with Recursion (Backtracking)

subtopics.name: Meet in the middle
subtopics.summary: Split the input into two halves, enumerate all 2^(n/2) possibilities for each half, and combine the halves with sorting + binary search, two pointers, or a hash map. Reduces 2^40 to about 2^20 * 20.
learn: Recognise it: n around 35-45 with subset-like choices, or a path whose two halves can be enumerated separately
Enumerate left-half sums into a sorted vector; for each right-half sum binary search / two-pointer the complement
For counting, use a hash map (or sorted + equal_range) of left-half values
Paths in a grid: enumerate from the start to the anti-diagonal and from the end back to it, meet on the diagonal
Mind memory: 2^20 values per half is fine; 2^23 of pairs can be tight
Modular / XOR variants combine with the same idea (sorted + lower_bound for 'max (a+b) mod m')

resources.title: USACO Guide: Meet In The Middle

subtopics.name: Sorting & using sorted order
subtopics.summary: Sorting makes equal values adjacent, puts extremes at the ends and enables greedy and two-pointer reasoning. Many easy problems become trivial once you realise the order of elements does not matter and you may sort.
learn: std::sort is O(n log n); sort(a.rbegin(), a.rend()) for descending
After sorting: count distinct values, find duplicates, take k largest/smallest, pair smallest with largest
Ask 'does the input order matter?' — if not, sort first
Sort pairs/tuples to sort by several keys lexicographically; keep original indices in the pair if you must output them
unique + erase to deduplicate a sorted vector

subtopics.name: Custom comparators & sorting by key
subtopics.summary: Sorting objects by a custom rule: by a derived key (a_i - b_i, remainder, value/weight), by several criteria, or by a rule that compares two items directly. Must define a strict weak ordering.
learn: Lambda comparator: sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const T& x, const T& y){ return x.key < y.key; })
Comparator must be strict: use <, never <=, or std::sort may crash
Sort by several criteria with tie-breakers, e.g. by score desc then index asc (or compare tuples)
Sort indices instead of objects (iota + sort by a[i]) to keep original positions
Derived keys: sort by a_i - b_i, by a_i mod k, by the result of a function
Avoid floating keys when a cross-multiplied integer comparison works

resources.title: USACO Guide: Custom Comparators and Coordinate Compression

subtopics.name: Coordinate compression & event sorting
subtopics.summary: Coordinate compression maps large or sparse values to 0..k-1 while keeping their order, so they can index arrays or BITs. Event sorting (a basic sweep line) turns intervals into +1/-1 events processed in sorted order.
learn: Compression: copy, sort, unique, then index = lower_bound(vals, x) - vals.begin()
Intervals [l, r]: events (l, +1) and (r+1, -1) (or (r, -1) with a tie-break) sorted by coordinate
Sweep through events keeping a running count to find maximum overlap or coverage lengths
Decide tie-breaking explicitly: do closings come before openings at the same coordinate?
Compression + Fenwick tree for counting inversions or 'number of earlier elements smaller than x'
A std::map can replace compression when only ordered iteration is needed

subtopics.name: 1D prefix sums
subtopics.summary: Precompute p[i] = a[1] + ... + a[i] so any range sum is p[r] - p[l-1] in O(1). The standard tool when a problem asks many range-sum queries or iterates over all subarrays.
learn: Use 1-indexed p with p[0] = 0 to avoid special cases
Range sum [l, r] = p[r] - p[l-1]; use long long
Prefix counts: keep a prefix array per character/property (e.g. count of 'a' in s[1..i])
Combine prefix and suffix arrays to evaluate 'remove one element' or 'split into two parts' options in O(1) each
Prefix sums of a boolean array answer 'how many good positions in [l, r]'

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Counting subarrays with prefix sums + hashing
subtopics.summary: Counting or detecting subarrays with a given sum/property by looking up earlier prefix values in a map: sum(l..r) = k iff p[r] - p[l-1] = k. Works with transformed arrays (a_i - 1, +1/-1, values mod m).
learn: For each r, add cnt[p[r] - k] to the answer, then increment cnt[p[r]]; start with cnt[0] = 1
Transform the array so the condition becomes 'sum equals 0' (e.g. a_i - 1 for sum = length, +1/-1 for balanced)
Divisibility: count pairs of equal p[i] mod m (normalise negatives with ((x % m) + m) % m)
Zero-sum subarray exists iff some prefix value repeats; greedy cut when a prefix repeats to break all zero-sum segments
Use std::map or a hashed unordered_map with a custom hash to avoid anti-hash tests

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Maximum subarray sum (Kadane)
subtopics.summary: Finding the best contiguous segment: best ending at i is max(a[i], best ending at i-1 + a[i]), or equivalently p[r] - min prefix before r. Variants add constraints such as a forced modification, a segment that must be proper, or multiplying one segment.
learn: Kadane: cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]); ans = max(ans, cur)
Equivalent view: answer = max over r of p[r] - min_{l<r} p[l]
Variant 'apply an operation to one subarray': track gain array and run Kadane on it
Variant with states (before / inside / after the modified segment) is a tiny DP
Decide whether the empty subarray is allowed
Length-bounded windows need sliding-window minimum of prefixes

resources.title: USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums (Max Subarray Sum)
cp-algorithms: Search the subarray with the maximum/minimum sum

subtopics.name: Difference arrays (range updates)
subtopics.summary: Applying many 'add x to [l, r]' updates offline: d[l] += x, d[r+1] -= x, then take the prefix sum of d. Also used to count how many intervals cover each point.
learn: Range add in O(1): d[l] += x; d[r+1] -= x; final value a[i] = prefix of d up to i
Counting coverage: each interval adds 1; after the prefix pass you know how many intervals cover each point
Can be nested: count how many times each operation is applied with one difference array, then apply operations with another
Combine with sorting: count how often each position is queried, then pair biggest counts with biggest values
Second-order differences handle adding arithmetic progressions to a range

resources.title: USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums (Difference Arrays)

subtopics.name: 2D prefix sums
subtopics.summary: Precomputing P[i][j] = sum of the rectangle (1,1)-(i,j) so any sub-rectangle sum is an O(1) inclusion-exclusion. Also extends to 2D difference arrays and to higher dimensions.
learn: 2D difference array: four corner updates, then a 2D prefix pass
Add a third dimension when values are small (e.g. one prefix table per brightness or per value)
Combine with binary search on the side length of a square
Weighted prefix sums (sum of i*a[i]) let you compute more complex aggregates in O(1)

resources.title: USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums (2D Prefix Sums)

subtopics.name: Prefix/suffix aggregates (xor, max, min, intersection)
subtopics.summary: Prefix and suffix arrays work for any associative operation: prefix XOR gives range XOR in O(1); prefix/suffix max/min/gcd/intersection let you evaluate 'everything except element i' or 'split point' questions quickly.
learn: Prefix XOR: xor(l..r) = px[r] ^ px[l-1] (XOR is its own inverse)
Prefix/suffix combination: value without element i = op(pre[i-1], suf[i+1])
Max/min/gcd are not invertible, so use prefix + suffix (or a sparse table) instead of subtraction
Interval intersection of all but one segment: prefix/suffix max of l and min of r
Counting subarrays with given XOR uses the same hash-map trick as sums

resources.title: USACO Guide: More on Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Two pointers on sorted arrays
subtopics.summary: Two indices moving monotonically through one or two sorted arrays: pair-sum search from both ends, merging two sorted lists, counting pairs with sum in a range. Total movement is O(n), so the whole scan is linear.
learn: Opposite ends: l = 0, r = n-1; if a[l] + a[r] > target then r-- else l++
Count pairs with sum <= x: for each l move r down while a[l] + a[r] > x
Pairs with sum in [L, R] = count(<= R) - count(<= L-1)
Merge-like scan over two sorted arrays (matching applicants to apartments, people to boats)
Prove why moving a pointer never skips the optimum (monotonicity)
Three values: fix one, two-pointer the other two in O(n^2)

subtopics.name: Variable-size sliding window
subtopics.summary: Maintaining a window [l, r] that expands to the right and shrinks from the left while a monotone condition holds (sum <= k, at most k distinct values, at most k zeros). Finds longest/shortest good subarrays or counts them in O(n).
learn: Requirement: if [l, r] is good then every sub-window is good (or every super-window is) — monotonicity
For each r, advance l while the window is bad; then [l, r] is the longest good window ending at r
Counting good subarrays: add (r - l + 1) for each r
Maintain window state incrementally: sum, frequency map, number of distinct values
'Exactly k' = 'at most k' - 'at most k-1'
Cyclic arrays: double the array and limit the window length to n

resources.title: USACO Guide: Sliding Window (With Two Pointers)

subtopics.name: Fixed-size window & sliding min/max (monotonic deque)
subtopics.summary: Processing every window of length k: add the new element, remove the old one. For window minimum/maximum use a monotonic deque (amortised O(1)); for medians/costs use two multisets. Frequently used to speed up DP transitions over a range.
learn: Fixed window: update aggregate with a[r] in and a[r-k] out instead of recomputing
Monotonic deque: pop back while back is worse than the new element, pop front when it leaves the window
Alternative: queue implemented with two stacks storing running minima
Sliding median / sliding cost: two balanced multisets (lower and upper half)
DP optimisation: dp[i] = min(dp[j]) + c over j in [i-k, i-1] becomes O(n) with the deque
Maximum subarray sum with length in [a, b]: prefix sums + sliding window minimum

subtopics.name: Binary search on a sorted array
subtopics.summary: Finding positions in a sorted array in O(log n): first element >= x, number of elements <= x, elements in a value range. The C++ tools are lower_bound and upper_bound.
learn: lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), x) -> first >= x; upper_bound -> first > x
Count of values in [L, R] = upper_bound(R) - lower_bound(L)
Answer many queries offline: sort once, binary search per query
Binary search over prefix sums / prefix maxima (they are monotone) to answer 'how far can I go' queries
std::set / multiset have their own .lower_bound — use the member function, not std::lower_bound (which is O(n) there)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Binary Search on a Sorted Array

problems.name: Queries about less or equal elements

subtopics.name: Binary search on the answer
subtopics.summary: If a yes/no predicate check(x) is monotone in x (false...false true...true), binary search for the boundary using O(log range) calls to check. Typical for 'minimise the maximum', 'maximise the minimum', or 'minimum time to finish'.
learn: Spot it: answers like 'minimum possible maximum' or 'largest x such that ...' with an easy feasibility check
Write check(x) first (often greedy), prove monotonicity, then binary search
Invariant template: lo always bad, hi always good; while (hi - lo > 1) { mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2; ... }
Choose bounds carefully (0 to 2e18 for time-type answers) and guard overflow inside check
Total complexity O(check * log(range))
Off-by-one: decide whether you search the first true or the last true

subtopics.name: Binary search on real numbers & averages
subtopics.summary: Binary searching a real-valued answer (time, radius, power, ratio) when the feasibility check is monotone. Also covers 'maximise the average/ratio' problems: average >= x iff sum(a_i - x) >= 0, so binary search x (fractional programming).
learn: Iterate a fixed number of times (60-100) instead of comparing with an epsilon; print with enough decimals (setprecision(10))
Pick safe bounds: lo surely feasible, hi surely infeasible (or vice versa); use long double when values reach 1e9+
Maximise average of a chosen subset/subarray: binary search x, subtract x from every element, check whether a valid choice has sum >= 0
Maximise a ratio sum(a)/sum(b): check whether max of sum(a_i - x*b_i) >= 0
Time-based checks: 'can everything be done/met by time t' with a simulation or geometry formula
If a closed formula exists, prefer it; otherwise binary search avoids fragile algebra

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Binary search (search on real numbers)
Codeforces EDU: Binary Search (real-valued answers and averages)

subtopics.name: k-th value & median binary search
subtopics.summary: Finding the k-th smallest value of a huge implicit multiset by binary searching the value x and counting how many elements are <= x. The same idea gives the 'median >= x' trick: map elements to +1/-1 relative to x so a median condition becomes a sum condition.
learn: k-th smallest: smallest x with count(<= x) >= k; count(<= x) must be computable quickly (formula, two pointers, sorted arrays)
Multiplication table: count(<= x) = sum over rows i of min(m, x / i)
Median >= x trick: b_i = (a_i >= x ? +1 : -1); median of a segment is >= x iff its b-sum is > 0 (adjust for the exact median definition)
Subarray with length >= k and positive b-sum: prefix sums + running minimum of p[j] for j <= i - k
Threshold binary search: find the value v such that taking every gain >= v uses about k operations, then fix up ties
Maximising the median of a construction: binary search the median, check greedily with the +1/-1 view

subtopics.name: Binary search with complex checks
subtopics.summary: Binary search on the answer where the feasibility check is itself a non-trivial algorithm: a greedy over the whole array, a DP, a simulation in time, or a two-dimensional reachability condition.
learn: Write and test check(x) as a standalone function before adding the binary search
Check may be DP or greedy over the whole array; total cost is O(check * log range)
Binary search on time with a movement/coverage simulation check (packmen, ships, robots)
Alternating constraints (odd/even positions) are checked greedily by trying both roles
Binary search on min and on max separately when minimising max - min
Watch overflow inside check (cap sums at the target)

subtopics.name: Ternary search on unimodal functions
subtopics.summary: Finding the minimum/maximum of a function that strictly decreases then increases (unimodal or convex). Ternary search narrows [l, r] by comparing f(m1) and f(m2); for integer convex functions, binary search on f(x+1) - f(x) is cleaner.
learn: Real version: m1 = l + (r-l)/3, m2 = r - (r-l)/3; drop the worse third; ~100-200 iterations
Integer version: binary search for the first x with f(x+1) - f(x) >= 0, or ternary until r - l < 3 then brute force
Requires strict unimodality — plateaus break it; sums of convex functions are convex
Classic sources: total distance/cost as a function of a meeting point or a target height, number of operations k vs cost
When f is convex in one variable and you iterate the other, nest the searches
Prove convexity (or test it with brute force) before relying on it

problems.name: Turtle vs. Rabbit Race: Optimal Trainings

subtopics.name: Bitwise operations & binary representation
subtopics.summary: Working with the binary form of integers using &, |, ^, ~, << and >>. Needed for subset masks, parity tricks and every problem that mentions AND/OR/XOR.
learn: Check bit i: (x >> i) & 1; set: x | (1 << i); clear: x & ~(1 << i); toggle: x ^ (1 << i)
Use 1LL << i for i >= 31; __builtin_popcount(ll), __builtin_ctz, __lg / 63 - __builtin_clzll for highest bit
x & (x - 1) removes the lowest set bit; x & -x isolates it; x is a power of two iff x && !(x & (x-1))
a & b <= min(a, b) <= max(a, b) <= a | b
Binary representation of n has floor(log2 n) + 1 bits; any number is a sum of distinct powers of two
Operator precedence: & | ^ bind weaker than == — always parenthesise

resources.title: USACO Guide: Intro to Bitwise Operators

subtopics.name: XOR properties & identities
subtopics.summary: XOR is addition without carry: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, it is associative and commutative and self-inverse. Many problems reduce to parity of bits, prefix XOR, or identities like a + b = (a ^ b) + 2(a & b).
learn: x ^ x = 0 lets you cancel pairs; XOR of a whole array is invariant under swapping
Prefix XOR: xor(l..r) = px[r] ^ px[l-1]
a + b = (a ^ b) + 2 * (a & b); a ^ b <= a + b; a ^ b and a + b have the same parity
If a ^ b = c then a ^ c = b — solve for the unknown by XOR-ing

Splitting into >= 2 parts with equal XOR: if the total XOR is 0 any split into two works; otherwise the number of parts must be odd and three parts (each equal to the total) suffice, since any three adjacent equal parts merge into one
Consecutive XOR 0 ^ 1 ^ ... ^ n has a period-4 closed form

resources.title: USACO Guide: Intro to Bitwise Operators (XOR)

problems.name: Vlad and a Pair of Numbers

subtopics.name: Per-bit independence & contribution counting
subtopics.summary: Bitwise operations act on each bit independently, so you can solve the problem separately for each of the ~30 bits and add up contributions (bit b contributes 2^b times the number of pairs/subarrays where it is set). Also: counting how often each bit is set across numbers.
learn: Sum over pairs of (a_i ^ a_j): for each bit, count ones c1 and zeros c0, add c1 * c0 * 2^b
Sum of AND/OR over subarrays: per bit, count subarrays that are all ones / contain a one
Operations that preserve the multiset of bits per position (AND/OR swaps) — reason with per-bit counts
Highest-bit grouping: a_i & a_j >= a_i ^ a_j iff they share the same highest bit
Counting ones in bit b among 1..n has a closed form (period 2^(b+1))
Use per-bit prefix counts to answer range AND/OR queries

resources.title: USACO Guide: Intro to Bitwise Operators

subtopics.name: Greedy bit-by-bit & AND/OR monotonicity
subtopics.summary: Building an answer from the highest bit down: a higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together, so fix bits greedily and check feasibility. Also uses the fact that prefix AND only decreases and prefix OR only increases, changing at most ~30 times.
learn: Greedy from the top bit: try to set bit b in the answer; keep it if the remaining budget/check allows
2^b > 2^(b-1) + ... + 1 justifies the greedy
AND over a growing range is non-increasing, OR is non-decreasing — binary search or two pointers apply
For a fixed right end there are at most log(maxA) distinct OR (or AND) values over left ends
Combine with masks: candidate answer mask must be a submask/supermask of chosen numbers
Powers of two: splitting/merging (like binary carries) handled bit by bit

resources.title: USACO Guide: Intro to Bitwise Operators

subtopics.name: Observations & small-case patterns
subtopics.summary: Problems with no standard algorithm: the solution is a key observation about the structure (what the answer can be, what never changes, what is always achievable). The skill is to experiment on small cases until the pattern appears, then prove it.
learn: Work small examples by hand or brute force n <= 8 and print the answers to spot a pattern
Ask: what is the answer at most? (often 0/1/2) What is a trivial lower/upper bound — is it always achievable?
Look at extremes: the maximum, the minimum, the first and last elements
Reformulate: what does one operation really change? What is the final state forced to look like?
Prove the observation (or at least stress-test it) before submitting
Keep a personal list of recurring tricks (sum/max conditions, endpoints matter, answer independent of order)

subtopics.name: Parity, invariants & monovariants
subtopics.summary: An invariant is a quantity that operations never change (sum mod 2, XOR, multiset of values at even positions); a monovariant only moves one way. Comparing invariants of the start and target states proves impossibility, and often also tells you exactly when it is possible.
learn: Find what an operation preserves: parity of the sum, sum mod k, total XOR, relative order of some elements
Parity of positions: swaps of distance 2 keep elements on positions of the same parity
Sum and max conditions: pairs can be removed iff sum is even and max <= sum - max
Monovariants (strictly decreasing potential) prove termination and bound the number of steps
If the invariant matches, usually build the transformation explicitly (connects to constructive)
Coloring arguments on grids (chessboard coloring) are invariants too

subtopics.name: MEX problems
subtopics.summary: MEX (minimum excluded non-negative integer) appears constantly in Div 2/3 problems. The key facts: MEX = k requires all of 0..k-1 to be present and k absent, only small values matter, and large or duplicate values can be reused freely.
learn: MEX of n numbers is at most n; values > n never change it
To get MEX >= k you need each of 0..k-1 at least once; extra copies are 'free' resources
Splitting into two sets: each value needs two copies to count for both sets (mex(A) + mex(B))
Operations that add x to an element: group values by remainder mod x and greedily fill 0, 1, 2, ...
Prefix MEX is non-decreasing; maintain it in O(n) total by advancing a pointer over a 'present' array
Games with MEX: count how often each small value appears (values appearing once are vulnerable)

subtopics.name: Pigeonhole & bounding the answer
subtopics.summary: If n items go into fewer than n boxes, two share a box. In contests this turns large inputs into trivial cases (n > m means two equal remainders, so the answer is immediate) and proves that the answer or the search is small, so brute force on the remaining cases is fast.
learn: n > m values mod m: two have equal remainder, so a difference (or a prefix-sum segment) is divisible by m
Among n + 1 prefix sums mod n, two coincide: some non-empty segment has sum divisible by n
Bounded number of distinct pair sums: brute force over pairs stops early because a collision must appear quickly
Answer is small because something grows fast (lcm of 1..k, doubling, factorial) — iterate only up to that bound
Combine: handle the large case with pigeonhole, the small case with brute force or DP

subtopics.name: Permutation cycles, swaps & inversion parity
subtopics.summary: A permutation splits into disjoint cycles (i -> p_i). Sorting by swaps needs n - (number of cycles) swaps, each swap changes the number of inversions by an odd amount, and 3-cycles preserve parity. These facts answer 'minimum swaps', 'is it reachable' and 'what is reachable from i' questions.
learn: Find cycles by following i -> p_i with a visited array; elements on a cycle share everything 'reachable' from them
Minimum swaps to sort a permutation = n - (number of cycles)
One swap changes the number of cycles by exactly +-1 and flips the parity of the permutation
Parity of a permutation = parity of inversions = parity of (n - cycles); 3-cycles are even, so they only reach same-parity permutations
Duplicates in the array give free parity flips (swap equal elements)
Bubble sort swaps = number of inversions; adjacent-swap distance between arrays = inversions

subtopics.name: Constructive basics
subtopics.summary: Instead of computing a number you output any object (array, string, permutation) with the required property. Start from the simplest pattern that might work, check it on edge cases, and output -1 exactly when an invariant forbids a solution.
learn: Try trivial constructions first: all equal, 1..n, alternating, sorted/reversed
Decide when the answer is impossible (parity, small n) and handle those cases explicitly
Build a solution for small n by hand and generalise (often by parity of n or n mod 4)
Write a checker that validates your output on random tests
Any valid answer is accepted — avoid over-engineering for optimality that is not asked

subtopics.name: Constructing permutations & arrays
subtopics.summary: Building permutations or arrays with constraints on adjacent differences, prefix values, fixed points, MEX or inversions. Common patterns: reverse blocks, interleave halves, shift by one, place large and small alternately.
learn: Cyclic shift (2, 3, ..., n, 1) removes all fixed points
Even numbers then odd numbers (2 4 6 ... 1 3 5 ...) keeps every adjacent difference >= 2 for n >= 4 (n = 2, 3 are impossible)
Fill positions greedily with the smallest/largest unused value (keep a set of unused values)
Reverse a suffix/prefix to adjust inversions or a target sum
Use prefix-max/MEX constraints to decide where a value is forced and fill the rest freely
Check small n (1, 2, 3) separately — they are often impossible

subtopics.name: Constructing grids & strings
subtopics.summary: Filling a grid or writing a string that satisfies local constraints (no equal neighbours, given row/column sums, avoided substrings). Patterns: chessboard colourings, cyclic shifts of rows, block repetition, periodic strings.
learn: Chessboard / striped colourings satisfy many 'adjacent cells differ' constraints
Shift each row cyclically by a constant to spread ones evenly (row/column count constraints)
Build a large grid from repeated small blocks (2x2 or 4x4) with offsets
Strings: periodic constructions (abcabc...) and trying all permutations of a few letters
Make a local change to an existing valid grid (change one cell per block) to satisfy an extra rule

subtopics.name: Constructing sequences of operations
subtopics.summary: Outputting a list of at most K operations (flip a prefix, swap, apply XOR, reverse) that transforms the input into a target. The limit K hints at the construction: n ops = fix one position per op, 2n ops = two ops per position, 3 ops = a clever fixed recipe.
learn: Read the operation limit as a hint about the per-element budget
Fix positions one by one from the end (or the start) so that later operations do not disturb them
Reduce to a canonical form (e.g. all zeros) from both start and target, then reverse the second sequence
Invariants decide feasibility; the construction must reach every state the invariant allows
Simulate your operations in the code to double-check the final state

subtopics.name: Arithmetic & number constructions
subtopics.summary: Constructing numbers or arrays with gcd/lcm/divisibility/sum constraints: split n into k parts with a given lcm, find numbers with prescribed remainders, choose values to make a sum vanish. Usually relies on parity or a simple divisor argument.
learn: Use 1s and 2s as fillers; handle n odd / n even / n mod 4 separately
gcd(x, x+1) = 1; lcm of (k, k, ...) patterns; divisibility by building from the previous term
Pairs (a, -b) and (b, -a) cancel: pair up elements to make a weighted sum zero
Choose numbers as multiples of a large base to control remainders
Verify with a brute-force checker on all small inputs

subtopics.name: Bitwise constructions (XOR/AND/OR)
subtopics.summary: Constructing numbers, pairs or permutations with a prescribed XOR/AND/OR value. Work bit by bit, use complements (x ^ (2^k - 1)) and powers of two as building blocks, and reserve one or two 'free' elements to fix the final XOR.
learn: Complement pairing: x and (2^k - 1) ^ x have AND 0 and OR 2^k - 1
Fix the XOR at the end: choose n - 1 elements freely, set the last to the XOR you still need (check distinctness/bounds)
Use large distinct high bits (2^29, 2^30) to make values distinct without disturbing low bits
Maximising OR under a sum: put 2^b - 1 (all low bits) in one element and the remainder in another
Permutations maximising alternating AND/OR: place the elements that hold the top bits at the end
Handle small n and targets of the form 2^m - 1 separately (they often need a special pattern)

resources.title: USACO Guide: Intro to Bitwise Operators

subtopics.name: Greedy basics
subtopics.summary: Making the locally best choice at each step (take the largest, use the cheapest, act as late as possible) when it can be shown never to hurt. The hard part is knowing when greedy fails; always try to find a counterexample first.
learn: State the greedy rule precisely, then try to break it with a small counterexample
Classic failure: coin change with arbitrary denominations — that needs DP
Proof idea 'stays ahead': after each step greedy is at least as good as any other solution
Moving everything to the median minimises total absolute distance
When greedy is unclear, brute-force small cases and compare

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms

subtopics.name: Greedy with sorting
subtopics.summary: Sort the items by the right key first, then a simple greedy pass becomes optimal: take cheapest items first, pair biggest with smallest, process tasks by deadline. Most Div 2 B/C greedy problems look like this.
learn: Find the processing order (by value, by deadline, by cost) and argue why it is optimal
Take-as-many-as-possible: sort ascending and add while the budget allows
Pairing: smallest with largest (two pointers) or adjacent after sorting
Prefix of the sorted order is often optimal — combine with prefix sums to try every count k
Minimising sum of |a_i - x|: choose x = median

resources.title: USACO Guide: Greedy Algorithms with Sorting

subtopics.name: Interval scheduling & covering
subtopics.summary: Classic interval greedies: choose the maximum number of disjoint intervals (sort by right end), stab all intervals with the fewest points, cover a segment with the fewest intervals, remove the fewest intervals so no point is over-covered.
learn: Max disjoint intervals: sort by right endpoint, take each interval that starts after the last chosen end
Min points to stab all intervals: sort by right end; place a point at r when the interval is not yet stabbed
Cover [0, L] with fewest intervals: repeatedly take the interval reaching furthest among those starting <= current end
Too many covering intervals at a point: drop the one that extends furthest right (set/priority queue)
Assigning values/rooms to intervals: sweep by left end, priority queue by right end
Nested segments: sort by l ascending and r descending

resources.title: USACO Guide: Greedy Algorithms with Sorting (Scheduling)

subtopics.name: Exchange argument
subtopics.summary: Proving a greedy order by showing that swapping two adjacent items that violate the order never makes the answer better. The comparison of the two orders usually yields the comparator itself (a_i * b_j < a_j * b_i, s + t < t + s).
learn: Take two adjacent items i, j; write cost(i then j) and cost(j then i); the sign of the difference is your comparator
Classic results: shortest processing time first, sort strings by s + t < t + s, sort by ratio a/b via cross-multiplication
Projects that raise and lower a resource: positives by requirement ascending, negatives by (requirement + change) descending
Check the comparator is transitive (strict weak order)
If no adjacent-swap argument works, the problem probably needs DP on top of the order

resources.title: USACO Guide: Greedy Algorithms with Sorting
cp-algorithms: Scheduling jobs on one machine
cp-algorithms: Scheduling jobs on two machines

subtopics.name: Lexicographic & digit greedy
subtopics.summary: Making the lexicographically smallest/largest string or number: decide characters from left to right, choosing the best possible character that still allows a valid completion. A monotonic stack often implements the 'remove k characters' family.
learn: Fix positions left to right; at each position pick the best character that keeps the rest feasible
Removing characters for the smallest result: monotonic stack, pop while top > current and removals remain
Merging two sequences while keeping internal order (e.g. by parity): two-pointer merge choosing the smaller head
First differing position decides — improve as early as possible
Digits: replace the first digit where improvement is possible, then keep improving while it helps

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms

subtopics.name: Greedy with priority queue / multiset
subtopics.summary: Greedy choices that need the current best among a changing set: always take the largest remaining value, assign the earliest free room, take the best k items in a prefix. A priority_queue or multiset gives each choice in O(log n).
learn: Sweep in one order (time, position) and keep candidates in a heap keyed by another criterion
Best k elements of every prefix: min-heap of size k, pop the smallest when it overflows
Repeatedly take the max, modify it and push it back (marginal gains when splitting into parts)
multiset supports erase(find(x)) and lower_bound — use it when you need both ends or arbitrary removals
Concatenate sorting + heap: sort by one parameter, heap over the other (e.g. length vs beauty)
Merging greedy (Huffman): repeatedly merge the two smallest items; total cost = sum of merge costs is minimised

subtopics.name: Regret greedy (undoable choices)
subtopics.summary: Greedily accept every choice, but keep enough information in a heap to undo the worst earlier choice when a better one arrives. Turns many seemingly DP problems (buy/sell stocks, drink potions, bracket costs) into O(n log n).
learn: Take the item now; if the constraint breaks, remove the worst taken item (heap top)
Potions: drink everything, if health < 0 spit out the most negative potion drunk so far
Buy low sell high: push price twice so a sale can later be 'upgraded' to a later sale
Bracket sequence with costs: start with cheapest bracket, switch the best candidate when balance goes negative
Proof: the heap keeps the optimal solution for each prefix — think of it as exchange argument applied online

subtopics.name: Interactive protocol & query thinking
subtopics.summary: In interactive problems your program talks to a judge: print a query, flush, read the response, and finish within a query limit. The query limit is the main hint about the intended strategy.
learn: Flush after every query: cout << ... << endl (or cout.flush()); read the response immediately
Stop immediately on a -1 response to avoid Idleness/Wrong Answer confusion
Count the query budget: n queries, n/2, log n or 2 log n each suggest a different strategy
Write a local interactor (or simulate the judge in a function) to test
Adaptive judges may change the hidden answer consistently with previous responses — your strategy must work in the worst case
Use randomisation when the judge is not adaptive and an expected bound suffices

resources.title: USACO Guide: Interactive and Communication Problems

subtopics.name: Binary search in interactive problems
subtopics.summary: The most common interactive pattern: the hidden object is found by halving the search space with each query. Variants use ternary splits, prefix queries, or need extra care to stay within ceil(log2 n) + c queries.
learn: Query ranges/prefixes so each answer halves the candidate set
With 20 queries and n = 1e5..1e6, think binary search; with 2 log n think nested or two-phase search
Ternary split (two queries per step dividing by 3) when each query compares two points
Cache previous answers to avoid repeating queries across many sub-searches
Prove the invariant on the candidate interval just like offline binary search

resources.title: USACO Guide: Interactive Problems (Divide and Conquer)

subtopics.name: Interactive with bit, XOR/AND/OR & pairing queries
subtopics.summary: Queries that return AND/OR/XOR/sum/gcd of hidden values. Typical tricks: a + b = (a ^ b) + 2(a & b) to recover sums, learn bits one by one, find a reference element (zero/max) and query everything against it, or process elements in pairs to save queries.
learn: Recover a + b from (a & b) and (a | b): a + b = (a & b) + (a | b)
Learn three values from three pairwise sums, then the rest relative to one known value
Find a special element (0, maximum, position of n) first, then use it as a reference
Bit-by-bit queries determine each bit of a hidden number in ~log(max) queries
Pairing/elimination: compare elements in pairs to keep only candidates (tournament style)
Sum of query limits like n + O(1) tells you each element can be queried about once
